title: Acids, Bases and Electrode Potentials

standard_text: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, pH of strong and weak acids and strong bases, Kw, Ka and pKa, buffer solutions, electrode potentials, standard e.m.f. of cells and predicting feasibility.
meta_desc: Free Year 13 A level chemistry worksheets on acids, bases and electrode potentials: pH of strong and weak acids, Kw, Ka and pKa, buffers, cell e.m.f. and feasibility. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

For a strong acid [H⁺] equals the acid concentration (twice for H₂SO₄). For a strong base use Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴. For a weak acid [H⁺] = √(Kac); for a buffer [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻].

The half-cell with the more negative E° is the negative electrode, where oxidation happens. E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative). A reaction is feasible if the oxidising agent has the more positive E°.

Example

pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl?

[H⁺] = 0.010

−log 0.010

Answer: 2.00

Example

Zn (−0.76 V) and Cu (+0.34 V) cell e.m.f.?

0.34 − (−0.76)

Answer: 1.10 V

Common mistakes

  • Using √(Ka c) for a strong acid.
  • Forgetting Kw for strong bases.
  • Subtracting the E° values the wrong way round.

faq.a: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, for example a weak acid with its salt.

faq.q: What does a positive E°cell mean?
faq.a: The cell reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
